newsitem.title: USA: U.N. mulls Iraqi spot oil sales as prices dip. [CORRECTED 16:05 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.N. mulls Iraqi spot oil sales as prices dip. [CORRECTED 16:05 GMT]

text.p: Less than a month before the first three-month tranche of the United Nations-Iraq oil-for-food deal is complete, the program's U.N. appointed overseers are mulling an allowance for additional spot sales due to plummeting world oil prices.

Western diplomats close to the plan said an overseer's report filed last week to the Iraq sanctions committee put the total value of the first three month's worth of contracts at about $800 million (corrects from $800,000).

Under terms of the oil deal, Iraq is permitted to sell $1 billion worth of crude from the December 10, 1996 start date to March 9, 1997, and then another $1 billion for the next 90 days for a total of $2 billion.

"The overseers are keeping an eye on the oil price, and will make a recommendation on how to proceed at some point. Current prices are quite a bit under the $1 billion, and since that last report prices have come down more," said a diplomat.
Overseers stopped approving formal oil contracts some weeks ago, trying to stay under the $1 billion cap.
The current total of approved contracts stands at 26, some of which cover 90 days and some 180 days.

For the first 90-day period, the U.N. is expected to allow Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organization (SOMO) to make up any shoftfall by selling additional oil on a spot basis, rather than agreeing new term contracts, diplomats said.

"I don't think (the overseers) would add another contract or change the existing contracts, it would be a one-off cargo to be sold on the spot market. The problem is not knowing where the oil price will be when the decision is made," said the source.
"It will be extremely difficult to hit the $1 billion mark (exactly)," said the diplomat.
Meanwhile, three of the 90-day contracts have already come before U.N. overseers for renewal for the second 90-day period, according to sources close to the overseers.
"They (the overseers) have said they will rubber-stamp contracts that come up for renewal as long as the terms aren't changed," said one source.

However, one of the three contracts up for renewal is at a reduced amount at SOMO's request and there is speculation that this reflects Baghdad's disappointment with the performance of some of the Russian contractors, sources said.
A number of contractors will be seeking to increase their amounts in the second 90-day period, particularly those cut back from original contract levels when prices were high.

Mitsubishi Corp, for example, will be looking to move back up to at least 40,000 barrels per day (bpd), the level of its contract before it was cut in half. Other contractors who were similarly cut back include Oil Energy of Italy, British Petroleum Co Plc and Texaco Inc.
The oil deal was put in place as a partial lifting of stringent sanctions clamped on Iraq in place since it invaded Kuwait in August, 1990.

Funds generated from oil sales are being sent to a special escrow account set-up in New York City at French bank Banque Nationale de Paris, where money will be drawn to pay for food, supplies and other costs.
The U.N. said this week that receipts from the oil sales had reached $386 million.
Iraq has routinely said that it will seek an increased amount of oil sales when it comes up for renewal, but the U.N. said it hasn't yet received any formal request.
